# OneCoin / Cryptoqueen Network: Investigative Reconstruction

## Executive assessment

The evidence supports a clear conclusion: OneCoin was presented as a cryptocurrency investment opportunity but was publicly characterized by U.S. authorities and prosecutors as a large-scale international fraud scheme operating through a global multi-level-marketing (“MLM”) structure. The scheme was founded and led by Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. According to the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”), the operation ran from approximately 2014 through 2019, was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, and induced investors worldwide to put more than $4 billion into the purported cryptocurrency. The available record further indicates that OneCoin’s value was represented as being governed by market supply and demand, while prosecutors alleged that it was instead set arbitrarily, and that the organization represented that it possessed a private blockchain even though no publicly verifiable blockchain existed. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The enforcement record is strongest regarding Greenwood. He was sentenced in the United States to 20 years’ imprisonment and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)) The DOJ also reports that more than $40 million in forfeited assets is currently available for compensation to eligible OneCoin victims. That amount should not be treated as the total amount forfeited from Greenwood personally; the evidence describes it as the pool of assets available through the broader OneCoin-related asset-forfeiture process. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

Ignatova’s status requires more careful treatment. The evidence establishes that she was identified by the DOJ as a co-founder and that the FBI has described her as a Top Ten Fugitive. The DOJ’s 2026 announcement states that law enforcement continues to pursue her and specifically refers to efforts to locate her. However, the supplied sources do not establish her current whereabouts, whether she is alive, or whether any particular reports about her disappearance or alleged death are true. The defensible conclusion is therefore that her location and present status remain unresolved in the supplied record. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

Two sources were provided:

| Source ID | Publisher and date | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice, April 13, 2026 | Primary government source describing the alleged scheme, victim compensation process, enforcement activity, fugitive status, and recovered assets |
| S2 | ArentFox Schiff, September 15, 2023 | Secondary legal-industry summary of Greenwood’s sentencing and the government’s allegations regarding OneCoin’s business model and representations |

S1 is the more authoritative source for current enforcement developments because it is an official DOJ announcement and directly addresses the compensation process, forfeiture proceeds, and the government’s continuing efforts concerning Ignatova. S2 is useful for details concerning Greenwood’s 2023 sentence and the specific misrepresentations attributed to the government, but it is a law-firm commentary rather than a charging document, verdict, sentencing memorandum, or judicial opinion. Accordingly, statements in S2 describing what prosecutors alleged should remain labeled as allegations or prosecutorial descriptions unless S1 independently confirms them.

## Chronology and development of the scheme

### Establishment and operating period

The DOJ states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It marketed and sold a cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a global MLM network. The DOJ identifies Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders and states that they, together with others, orchestrated the investment scheme between 2014 and 2019. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

S2 provides additional context, stating that OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The supplied record does not provide a precise date for the U.S. launch, identify a specific U.S. corporate entity responsible for that expansion, or describe the full international corporate structure. The appropriate characterization is therefore that the operation had a Bulgarian base, expanded internationally, and had a U.S. presence by approximately 2015 according to the secondary source. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Investment solicitation and MLM structure

The central distribution mechanism was a global MLM network. According to the DOJ, OneCoin members were able to receive commissions for recruiting other individuals to purchase cryptocurrency packages. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) S2 similarly describes a structure in which members recruited others to buy packages and states that Greenwood was OneCoin’s top MLM distributor. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

This distinction is significant. The available evidence does not describe OneCoin merely as a failed cryptocurrency project or a conventional investment whose value unexpectedly collapsed. Instead, it describes a system in which the sale of packages and recruitment of additional participants were central to revenue generation and compensation. The record supports identifying recruitment incentives and package sales as core operational features, but it does not provide enough information to map the full hierarchy of distributors, compensation tiers, or the identity and roles of all other senior participants.

### Representations concerning value and blockchain technology

S2 reports that prosecutors alleged OneCoin represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand, while its value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

S2 also reports that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions, although no public, verifiable blockchain actually existed. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

These facts should be described as the government’s allegations as summarized by S2, not as independently established technical findings in the sources supplied here. The DOJ’s 2026 release does, however, characterize OneCoin as a “fraudulent cryptocurrency” and states that victims were induced to invest as a result of misrepresentations. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Principal founders and roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin and states that she participated with Greenwood and others in orchestrating the international investment scheme. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The supplied sources do not provide a detailed organizational job title for Ignatova beyond “co-founder.” They do not, for example, establish from the provided material whether she formally served as chief executive officer, controlled a particular subsidiary, designed the alleged technology, or managed a specific geographic market. Such roles should not be inferred. The supported finding is that Ignatova was a principal founder and senior figure associated with the scheme.

The DOJ further states that the FBI considers Ignatova an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and that law enforcement continues efforts to locate her. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) S2 states that she remains at large and was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The evidence identifies Karl Sebastian Greenwood as OneCoin’s other co-founder. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) S2 describes him as a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom, OneCoin’s top MLM distributor, and an individual alleged to have earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The $300 million figure is presented in S2 as an allegation concerning Greenwood’s earnings. It should not be confused with the approximately $300,000 forfeiture order imposed in connection with his sentence. S2 states that Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

Greenwood is the principal founder for whom the supplied record contains a completed U.S. criminal enforcement outcome: a 20-year prison sentence and a forfeiture order. The sources provided do not state the specific statutory counts of conviction, the sentencing court’s full reasoning, or whether the sentence has been modified on appeal.

## Scale and victim impact

The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide in OneCoin between 2014 and 2019. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) S2 gives a similar figure and estimates approximately 3.5 million investors. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The $4 billion figure is supported by both sources, while the 3.5 million-investor figure appears only in S2. It should therefore be reported as a figure included in the secondary summary rather than as an independently corroborated number within the supplied record. Neither source supplies a country-by-country breakdown, a calculation of net investor losses, or a distinction between principal invested and amounts withdrawn or recovered.

The DOJ’s compensation announcement states that more than $40 million in forfeited assets is available for victim compensation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) Eligible individuals are described as those who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019. The source states that Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as remission administrator and that the DOJ’s Criminal Division Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the process. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The sources also state that no payment is required to participate in the remission process. This warning is relevant because the DOJ specifically cautions victims about impersonators claiming to represent the federal government or the remission administrator. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Enforcement status and unresolved issues

### Established enforcement facts

The supplied record establishes the following enforcement facts:

1. The DOJ has pursued multiple OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))
2. Greenwood received a 20-year prison sentence. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))
3. Greenwood was ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))
4. More than $40 million in forfeited assets is currently available for victim compensation through the DOJ remission process. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))
5. The FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation conducted the criminal fraud investigation, with assistance from the DOJ Office of International Affairs. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

### Ignatova’s status

The evidence does not resolve Ignatova’s current physical or legal status beyond identifying her as a fugitive whom authorities continue to seek. The DOJ’s wording—stating that the FBI continues its investigative pursuit and efforts to locate her—supports the conclusion that she has not been publicly brought into custody in the record supplied. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

S2 uses the phrase “remains at large” and notes her placement on the FBI Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)) Neither source provides evidence confirming where she is, whether she is alive, or whether allegations concerning her fate have been substantiated. Therefore, any claim that she is dead, hiding in a particular country, protected by specific individuals, or otherwise definitively located would exceed the evidence supplied.

## Conclusion

The public record supplied here supports a concrete assessment: OneCoin was an international investment-fraud operation organized around the sale of a purported cryptocurrency and amplified through MLM recruitment. Ignatova and Greenwood were its principal founders. Greenwood’s role is further associated with top-level distribution and alleged financial benefit, and his criminal case concluded with a 20-year sentence and forfeiture order. The scheme’s scale exceeded $4 billion in worldwide investments, while the current remission pool exceeds $40 million.

The record does not justify treating all reported details as equally proven. Greenwood’s sentence and the existence of the remission process are enforcement facts. The claims about arbitrary valuation, the absence of a public blockchain, Greenwood’s alleged $300 million earnings, and the estimated 3.5 million investors are presented as prosecutorial or secondary-source descriptions and should retain those qualifications. Ignatova’s status is unresolved: she is documented as a co-founder and FBI Top Ten Fugitive whom authorities continue to seek, but the supplied evidence does not establish her current whereabouts or ultimate fate.

## References

ArentFox Schiff. (2023, September 15). *Co-founder of fraudulent cryptocurrency sentenced to 20 years in prison*. Investigations Blog. [https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)
